domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The talk centers on recording and replaying agent execution traces for production debugging and postmortem root cause analysis, which is core observability and reliability for LLM agent systems. Speakers are from Microsoft's enterprise Commerce and Ecosystem Data Platform team building production agent systems, and Chronicle is developer infrastructure for debugging agent workflows. The talk addresses production failure debugging and replay-based testing using recorded traces as deterministic test cases. Requires familiarity with agentic workflow architecture and understanding of non-determinism concepts in LLM systems. A conference presentation with live demos of a proof-of-concept recording and replay tool. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: The talk opens with the common scenario of an agent failing in production in a way that cannot be reproduced, leaving teams unable to debug or guarantee it won't recur. A stock-selling agent example illustrates this: asked to sell $1,000 of stock, the agent interprets 1,000 as the quantity field, selling 1,000 shares at $190 each—a $190,000 disaster that returns a clean 200 OK in 30 milliseconds with zero exceptions or alerts. The standard reflex of setting temperature to zero is debunked through four first-principles arguments: sampling determinism is not system determinism; floating point math is not associative; the real issue is batch invariance, not concurrency; and mixture-of-experts routing has capacity limits causing token rerouting dependent on co-batched traffic. The speakers clarify that chasing identical text outputs is the wrong goal—teams need identical state transitions, not model determinism. They distinguish bitwise determinism (same input, same output—controllability you neither get nor want from hosted APIs) from replayability (re-validating a past run well enough to debug—observability achieved by recording, not freezing, the model). Recording should happen at node boundaries, capturing what enters and leaves each step, not at the network layer where local retrieval, in-process tools, and memory never touch the network. Chronicle, a proof-of-concept tool built around boundary annotations, records all input/output pairs plus metadata like model and code version, freezing the entire run as a trace. Chronicle also uses recorded traces as test cases: by stubbing unchanged nodes and running modified nodes live, engineers can verify fixes deterministically without calling the model. The talk distinguishes deterministic testing (guardrails, tool calls—where Chronicle shines) from behavioral testing (tone, trajectory correctness—better served by LLM-as-a-judge techniques). The closing key takeaways are: stop chasing bitwise determinism through the API; log session variables like LLM version, build ID, and RAG chunks; capture the full envelope, not just the prompt; use replay to debug and then reuse the same trace as a test case; and keep generation-time variation alive—don't pin temperature to zero, since that is what brings agency into your agent.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Reproducibility Problem and Stock Agent Example
sections.summary: Introduces the core problem: agents fail in production in ways that can't be reproduced. A stock-selling agent mistook $1,000 as quantity, selling 1,000 shares at $190 each—a $190,000 error with clean 200 OK, zero exceptions, and green dashboards.

sections.title: Why Temperature Zero Fails: Four First Principles
sections.summary: Debunks the misconception that temperature zero ensures determinism through four arguments: sampling determinism isn't system determinism, floating point math isn't associative, batch invariance is the real culprit not concurrency, and MOE routing reroutes tokens based on co-batched traffic.

sections.title: Bitwise Determinism vs Replayability
sections.summary: Distinguishes bitwise determinism (controllability, same input same output, not achievable or desirable from hosted APIs) from replayability (observability, re-validating a past run for debugging). The right question is how to debug an unreproducible run, not how to make the model deterministic.

sections.title: Where to Record and the Workflow Loop
sections.summary: Advocates recording at node boundaries (what enters and leaves each step) rather than the network layer. Introduces the end-to-end loop: annotation, recording, visualization, understanding, fixing, replaying, verifying.

sections.title: Chronicle and Boundary Annotation Demo
sections.summary: Introduces Chronicle, a proof-of-concept tool using boundary annotations as bounding boxes around any node (tool, LLM, RAG). Records all input/output pairs plus model and code version metadata. Demonstrates recording the stock agent trace showing the LLM mistaking 1,000 as quantity.

sections.title: Replay-Based Testing with Stubbing and Assertions
sections.summary: Demonstrates Chronicle's replay mode: loading a recorded trace, stubbing unchanged nodes, running modified nodes live, and asserting on outputs. Distinguishes deterministic testing (guardrails, tool calls—free and rerunnable via Chronicle) from behavioral testing (tone, trajectory correctness), where LLM-as-a-judge is better suited.

sections.title: Key Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Presents five final takeaways: stop chasing bitwise determinism through the API; log session variables (LLM version, build ID, RAG chunks); capture the full envelope, not just the prompt; use replay to debug and reuse the same trace as a test case; and keep generation-time variation alive—don't pin temperature to zero, since that is what brings agency. A QR code provides access to Chronicle code and articles. Closing remark: traces you put in your agent today make your on-call cycle tomorrow much better.
